name: Kṛṣṇānanda Āgamavāgīśa
summary: Bengali tantric scholar of Navadvīpa, compiler of the Tantrasāra (Bṛhattantrasāra), the standard Bengali digest of tantric worship, which sets out the meditation and worship of Dakṣiṇakālī. Bengali tradition credits him with fixing the popular form of Dakṣiṇakālī and with introducing the worship of Kālī in clay images in the household.

tradition.text: A contemporary (some say a fellow student) of Caitanya

realization_account.text: Bengali legend: praying to know the form in which Kālī should be worshipped, he was told to adopt the first form he saw at dawn; he saw a dark village woman plastering a wall, her hair loose, who bit her tongue in embarrassment on seeing him — the pose of Dakṣiṇakālī.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: The legend is oral/popular; the Tantrasāra itself quotes the Kālī Tantra's older meditation verse (tea:tantrasara-krsnananda:2.syama-dhyana).

name: Sarvānanda (Sarvānandanātha) of Mehar
summary: Śākta adept of Mehar (Chandpur/Comilla, East Bengal), remembered as having realised all ten Mahāvidyās in a single night; the Sarvollāsa Tantra is ascribed to him and his descendants were Śākta gurus in Bengal.

realization_account.text: On a new-moon night at Mehar, seated on a corpse-seat with the help of his servant Pūrṇānanda, he had the vision of all ten Mahāvidyās one after another (hence 'Sarvavidyā').
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: The servant Pūrṇānanda of this story is not Pūrṇānanda Giri, author of the Śrītattvacintāmaṇi.

name: Brahmānanda Giri
summary: Sixteenth-century Bengali Śākta teacher and author of the Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī and (traditionally) the Tārārahasya; remembered as the guru of Pūrṇānanda.

name: Pūrṇānanda Giri (Paramahaṃsa)
summary: Bengali Śākta renunciant of the sixteenth century, author of the Śrītattvacintāmaṇi (1577), whose sixth chapter is the Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa, the classic account of the six centres and the ascent of kuṇḍalinī; also of the Śyāmārahasya on Kālī worship, the Śāktakrama and the Kulavṛtti. Remembered as a disciple of Brahmānanda Giri.

name: Rāmprasād Sen
summary: Bengali Śākta poet-saint of Kumārhaṭṭa (Halisahar), whose songs to Kālī and Umā (the 'Rāmprasādī' songs) created Bengal's devotional Śākta tradition: the devotee as the Mother's child who claims, reproaches and surrenders to her, and who treats Kālī's name as the refuge at death. Patronised by Rājā Kṛṣṇacandra of Nadia, who gave him the title Kavirañjana; author of a Vidyāsundara and a Kālīkīrtana.

realization_account.text: Working as a clerk in Calcutta he filled his account book with songs to the Mother; his employer, moved, sent him home with a stipend. The Mother came in the form of his little daughter to help him mend a fence; he died while immersing Kālī's image in the Ganges, singing.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Biographical legends are from 19th-century Bengali tradition; dates vary by source.

name: Kamalākānta Bhaṭṭācārya
summary: Bengali Śākta poet and sādhaka of Ambikā-Kālnā, later at Burdwan under Mahārāja Tejcandra; author of Śyāmā-saṅgīt to Kālī and Umā in the line of Rāmprasād, and of the Sādhaka-rañjana on tantric yoga.

realization_account.text: The Mahārāja of Burdwan became his disciple after he showed that the Goddess answered his call.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Jñānānanda Paramahaṃsa
summary: Author of the Kaulāvalīnirṇaya, a digest of Kaula practice.

name: Narasiṃha Ṭhakkura
summary: Maithila scholar, author of the Tārābhaktisudhārṇava, a large digest on the worship of Tārā.

name: Rāmatoṣaṇa Vidyālaṅkāra
summary: Bengali pandit who compiled the Prāṇatoṣiṇī, a vast compendium of tantric passages (c. 1820).

name: Hariharānanda Bhāratī (Hariharānandanātha Tīrthasvāmī)
summary: Bengali Kaula avadhūta and commentator of the Mahānirvāṇa Tantra; associated with Rammohun Roy, who cited the Mahānirvāṇa. Some scholars suggest the Mahānirvāṇa was composed in his circle; the tradition regards it as revealed scripture.
notes: Attribution of the Mahānirvāṇa's composition to him is a scholarly hypothesis only; recorded as 'disputed'.

name: Vimalaprabodha
summary: Author of Nepalese Kubjikā ritual works (Paścimārcanapaddhati, Mahārahasyasaṃpradāya) preserved in the Muktabodha collection.
notes: Known only from catalogue attribution; date unknown.

name: Vimalānanda Svāmī
summary: Commentator on the Karpūrādistotra (Hymn to Kālī) whose commentary Avalon translated.

name: Mahākāla
summary: Śiva as 'Great Time', Kālī's consort in the Kālīkula (Toḍala 1.3); speaker of the Karpūrādistotra and revealer of Kālī tantras in the tradition's account.

name: Bāmākhepā (Vāmākṣepā)
summary: Śākta 'mad saint' of the Tārāpīṭh cremation ground in Birbhum, devotee of Tārā, who lived as a child of the Mother, disregarding rules of purity; remembered for his miracles and for teaching by paradox.

realization_account.text: Taught by the ascetic Kailāspati Bābā at Tārāpīṭh, he had the vision of Tārā in the cremation ground and thereafter treated her as his mother.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: The Bhairavī Brāhmaṇī (Yogeśvarī)
summary: Wandering woman tantric adept who taught Ramakrishna the sixty-four tantric sādhanas at Dakshineswar (1861–63) and declared his states to be those of an incarnation, in the Ramakrishna tradition's account.

name: Śivacandra Vidyārṇava Bhaṭṭācārya
summary: Bengali Śākta pandit and guru, author of the Tantratattva (translated as 'Principles of Tantra'), and teacher of Sir John Woodroffe (Arthur Avalon), through whom many Kaula and Kālī texts were printed.

name: Mukundarām Cakravartī (Kavikaṅkaṇa)
summary: Bengali poet of the Caṇḍīmaṅgala, the most famous narrative poem of the goddess Caṇḍī.

name: Bhāratcandra Rāy (Rāyguṇākar)
summary: Court poet of Rājā Kṛṣṇacandra of Nadia, author of the Annadāmaṅgala in praise of Annapūrṇā.
